evidence.title: FDA authorization of AI-enabled medical devices
evidence.text: AI-enabled software that meets the definition of a medical device must be authorized by the US FDA before it is marketed, through 510(k) clearance, De Novo classification or premarket approval. In December 2024 the FDA finalized guidance on predetermined change control plans that lets makers pre-specify how an AI model will be updated after authorization.

evidence.title: Radiology dominates authorized AI medical devices
evidence.text: The FDA's public list of AI-enabled medical devices passed 1,000 authorizations by 2025, and roughly three quarters are in radiology. Typical tools detect findings on chest X-rays, CT scans and mammograms or flag suspected urgent cases, such as brain bleeds, for prioritized review by a radiologist.

evidence.title: WHO guidance on AI ethics in health
evidence.text: In June 2021 the World Health Organization published 'Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health', setting out six principles including protecting human autonomy, ensuring transparency and fostering accountability.

evidence.title: Meta leans harder on AI-ranked feeds

The core theme of the discussion centered on how AI agents are changing asynchronous work and documentation within distributed teams. Lucas Ferreira explained that the biggest shift is that agents can turn async content into queryable information, allowing teams to ask questions about decisions and receive direct links to relevant memos. Hannah Okafor shared a practical example of this, noting that decision memos are now used by new hires to quickly find the right information, which resulted in onboarding time dropping from three weeks to about two. Lucas emphasized that agents amplify existing knowledge, meaning good documentation becomes more useful, while poor documentation risks being confidently repeated. Hannah raised a human risk, pointing out that if agents handle status updates, the reflective process of writing—which can reveal problems through silence—might be lost. Lucas also noted that agents could exacerbate surveillance issues if companies monitor activity data, advocating for using agents to help people rather than watch them. Regarding the listener question of whether agents will replace remote workers, Lucas predicted that AI agents will mostly replace tasks like summarizing and routing, benefiting those who already work in a documented, asynchronous manner. Both speakers concluded that the key takeaway is intention; successful outcomes stem from teams deliberately deciding how they work rather than drifting into processes."}
